data.title: Coastal Wetland Restoration
data.short_summary:
Enhanced sequestration in above-ground biomass and soil carbon from restoration activities in coastal wetlands (mangroves and tidal marshes).

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.
data.description:
Two ecosystems were assessed for Coastal Wetland Restoration: Mangrove Restoration and Tidal Marsh Restoration.

Mangrove Restoration

This layer shows the climate benefit, as avoided further CO2 emissions from soils and additional sequestration from aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, and soils, resulting from restoring degraded or converted mangrove ecosystems. These estimates are based on a global dataset on restorable areas (Worthington, in prep) and drivers of loss (Goldberg et al., 2022), sequestration rates from the IPCC for aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, and soil organic carbon as well as emissions using soil organic carbon stocks (Maxwell et al., 2023), and emissions factors (Sasmito et al., 2019). 

Tidal Marsh Restoration

This layer shows the climate benefit, as avoided further CO2 emissions from soils, and additional sequestration from soils, resulting from restoring degraded or converted tidal marsh ecosystems. These estimates are based on estimates of global restoration potential (2.7% of observed extent, from Buelow et al., 2022), sequestration rates from the IPCC for soil organic carbon as well as emissions using soil organic carbon stocks (Maxwell et al., 2024), and emissions factors (McTigue et al., 2021). 

Consistent with the naturebase accounting framework, areas of overlap between cropland and non-cropland pathway extents were resolved using a proportional allocation approach. Cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the fraction of each 1 km² pixel classified as cropland, while non-cropland pathway mitigation was weighted by the inverse proportion. For a detailed description of this methodology, see Section I(c), Cropland Extent, in the NCS Accounting Rules Narrative.

Units: all raster data (.tif) are in tCO2e/ha/yr. All tabular data (.csv) are summarised in tCO2e/yr.

To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) of the NCS implementation extent in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the NCS hectare extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_ha
3) Divide the mitigation value by the NCS hectare extent: tCO2e/ha/yr = [pathway]_tco2e / [pathway]_ha*

*FLAG: As this is the hectares of NCS extent of the 1km2 raster, extent may be over-estimated. Use with caution. These area estimates are not recommended for pathways that have extents finer than 1km resolution



To calculate the per hectare mitigation potential (density) for each administrative area* in tCO2e/ha/yr: 
1) Find the total mitigation value: this is provided in the spreadsheet as [pathway]_tco2e
2) Find the administrative extent: This is provided in the spreadsheet as 'admin_ha'
3) Divide the mitigation value by the administrative extent: tCO2e/ha/yr in each administrative area = [pathway]_tco2e / admin_ha

*This is useful for comparison between administrative areas

Please consult the download package under 'Download Now' for comprehensive metadata and a detailed description.

data.data_caveats:
Mangrove Restoration

Our estimates of potential restorable area were based on data from 1996-2020. It is important to note that there have been mangrove areas lost pre- 1996 that may be opportunities for restoration, but they are not included here due to data limitations. We had a slight temporal mismatch between our loss data (1996-2020) and our data on the loss drivers used to exclude loss areas resulting from erosion and settlement (2000-2016). We assumed that 73% of the soil organic carbon remained in the soils after conversion across all loss areas even though this value would change based on the year of loss as well as the driver of loss. We also incorporated the same sequestration rate across all geographies due to lack of data on regionally-specific sequestration rates. We also did not apply a background recovery rate due to lack of data.  

Tidal Marsh Restoration

Our estimates of potential restorable area were based global modeled outputs and are only applied in areas that are adjacent to existing tidal marsh (e.g., within the bounds of the current extent map). We also did not exclude from our potentially restorable areas, those areas that are particularly vulnerable to sea level rise or those areas that have been converted to urban areas or permanent settlements. The tidal marsh extent map is also constrained to areas within 60°N and 60° S latitudinal limits (e.g., the limits of the Sentinel satellite imagery).
data.authors: Lindsey S. Smart, Judith Ament, Tom Worthington, Tania Maxwell
data.approach_and_methods:
Mangrove Restoration

To estimate mangrove restoration potential, we quantify the extent of restorable land within a 1km-cell grid using the union of Global Mangrove Watch mangrove extent maps between 1996 and 2020 (Bunting et al., 2022). Excluded from the restorable land area is the current 2020 mangrove extent and any areas lost due to urbanization and erosion (assuming these cannot be restored) based on an assessment of the global drivers of mangrove loss (Goldberg et al., 2020). This potentially restorable area dataset is currently in preparation for publication (Worthington et al., in review). We then estimate the avoided loss of remaining carbon stocks within the restorable land area by assuming that approximately 73% (or half of the 54% from Sasmito et al., 2019 has already been emitted prior to restoration intervention) of the original soil organic carbon stocks (estimated using Maxwell et al., 2023) remain. With that remaining SOC, we assume another 27% of CO2 is emitted using the 2035-time horizon, which is included in our mitigation benefit of restoration. In addition to this, we include annual sequestration rates for the restorable land area using the average aboveground biomass growth rate from the IPCC (10.4 Mg/ha/yr), converted to carbon using conversion factor 0.48 (Kauffman et al.  ,2020), the annual belowground biomass growth rate (6.032 Mg/ha/yr) derived from the IPCC’s average root-to-shoot ratio (0.58) and converted to carbon using 0.47 conversion factor, and soil organic carbon accumulation rate of 1.62 MgC/ha/yr (IPCC, 2014).  

Tidal Marsh Restoration

To estimate tidal marsh restoration potential, we quantified the extent of restorable land within a 1km-cell grid using global estimates of restoration potential which estimate that approximately 2.7% of the observed extent is restorable (Buelow et al., 2022).  Grid cells with greater than 75% intact tidal marsh extent were excluded from the restorable land area. We then estimate the avoided loss of remaining carbon stocks within the restorable land area by assuming that approximately 50% (Griscom et al., 2017) of the organic carbon stocks (estimated using Maxwell et al., 2024) remain. With that remaining SOC, we assume another 15.5%/yr of CO2 (McTigue et al., 2021) is emitted through 2035, which is included in our mitigation benefit of restoration. In addition to this, we include annual sequestration rates for the restorable land area using the average soil organic carbon accumulation rate of 0.91 MgC/ha/yr (IPCC, 2014).
data.additionality:
Mangrove Restoration

We only considered restorable areas as areas lost from 1996 onward even though areas lost pre-1996 might be restorable but they are excluded because the soil organic carbon remaining in their soils may be minimal or zero. We also did not include areas lost due to erosion or settlement as ‘restorable’. Although not included in this version due to lack of data, a background recovery rate could be applied to ensure additionality only for the regrowth occurring as a result of restoration activity. We also assumed that some CO2 emitted prior to restoration interventions could not be included in the climate mitigation benefit and assumed that not all of the remaining carbon in the soils would be emitted as CO2 within the time horizon we are considering.  

Tidal Marsh Restoration

We are only looking at restoration potential in areas that have experienced loss in the last 20 years.
data.next_steps:
Mangrove Restoration

In the near-term, we would like to more realistically represent the carbon that remains after conversion by assigning the percentage of organic carbon remaining in the soils according to the emissions factors associated with the majority loss driver within the administrative units. 

Tidal Marsh Restoration

We would like to incorporate spatially-explicit information on losses to better constrain restoration opportunities and also exclude areas that are no longer ‘restorable’ due to erosion from sea level rise or conversion to urban areas or permanent settlements.
